dmm-2011-team-01.title: Fermat's two-squares theorem
dmm-2011-team-01.body:
A sum of two squares is $0,1$ or $2$ modulo $4$, so a prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$ is never a sum of two squares. By Fermat's theorem every prime $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is a sum of two positive squares, and $2=1^2+1^2$.

The primes below $100$ that are $1$ mod $4$ are $5,13,17,29,37,41,53,61,73,89,97$ ($11$ primes). Adding $2$ gives $12$.

**Answer: 12**

dmm-2011-team-02.title: Parametrize the triples
dmm-2011-team-02.body:
Every Pythagorean triple is $k(m^2-n^2,\,2mn,\,m^2+n^2)$ with $m>n$ coprime and of opposite parity. Its perimeter is $2km(m+n)$, so $km(m+n)=1000$.

Try $m=4,n=1$: $m(m+n)=20$ divides $1000$, with $k=50$. This gives the triple $50\cdot(8,15,17)=(400,750,850)$, with sum $2000$. (The problem states this is the only one.)

Then $a+c-b=400+850-750=500$. Equivalently $a+c-b=10k=500$.

**Answer: 500**

dmm-2011-team-03.title: Two antipodal points and an equilateral triangle
dmm-2011-team-03.body:
Put the sphere's centre at the origin. Two points $u,v$ on the unit sphere are at distance at least $\sqrt2$ exactly when $u\cdot v\le0$. So we have five unit vectors $v_1,\dots,v_5$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with all pairwise dot products $\le0$.

*Claim: two of them are antipodal.* Five vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ satisfy a nontrivial relation $\sum c_iv_i=0$. Split it as $P=N$ with $P=\sum_{c_i>0}c_iv_i$, $N=\sum_{c_j<0}|c_j|v_j$. Then $|P|^2=P\cdot N=\sum c_i|c_j|\,v_i\cdot v_j\le0$, so $P=N=0$. Hence some nonempty set $I$ of the vectors has a relation $\sum_{i\in I}c_iv_i=0$ with all $c_i>0$; take $I$ minimal.

* $|I|=2$: $v_i=-v_j$, an antipodal pair.
* $|I|=3$: the three vectors are coplanar, spanning a plane $\Pi$. For each remaining vector $u$, $u\cdot v_i\le0$ and $\sum c_i\,u\cdot v_i=0$ force $u\cdot v_i=0$ for all $i\in I$, so $u\perp\Pi$. The two remaining vectors are unit vectors perpendicular to $\Pi$ with $u\cdot w\le0$, hence antipodal.
* $|I|=4$: the four vectors span $\mathbb R^3$, and the fifth vector $u$ would satisfy $u\cdot v_i=0$ for all $i\in I$ in the same way, so $u=0$, impossible.
* $|I|=5$ is impossible for a minimal relation in $\mathbb R^3$ (the vectors would span a $4$-dimensional space).

So two points are antipodal poles $\pm n$, and each of the other three points $x$ satisfies $x\cdot n\le0$ and $x\cdot(-n)\le0$, so $x\cdot n=0$: the three points lie on the equator.

*Volume.* The convex hull of the poles and three equator points has volume $\frac23\cdot[\text{area of the part of the equatorial disc cut out by the hull}]$, namely $\frac23\cdot\text{area}\big(\operatorname{conv}(T\cup\{0\})\big)$ where $T$ is the set of three equator points. If the gaps between consecutive points (as angles) are $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2\pi$, this area is $\frac12(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)$ when all gaps are at most $\pi$, which is at most $\frac32\sin\frac{2\pi}3=\frac{3\sqrt3}4$ by concavity of $\sin$ on $[0,\pi]$; if one gap exceeds $\pi$ the area is at most $1$. So the volume is at most $\frac23\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

This is attained by the poles and an equilateral triangle on the equator (all distances are $\sqrt2$ or $\sqrt3$).

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$**

dmm-2011-team-04.title: Cut into four triangles
dmm-2011-team-04.body:
Triangle $ACE$ is equilateral with side $6$, so its area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot36=9\sqrt3$. The hexagon is $ACE$ together with the three triangles $ABC$, $CDE$, $EFA$, each with sides $5,5,6$. Such a triangle has height $\sqrt{25-9}=4$ on the base $6$, hence area $12$.

Total area: $9\sqrt3+3\cdot12=36+9\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $36+9\sqrt3$**

dmm-2011-team-05.title: Modular inverses
dmm-2011-team-05.body:
There are $11\cdot11=121$ equally likely outcomes. Since $11$ is prime, each $X\in\{1,\dots,10\}$ has exactly one $Y$ in $\{1,\dots,10\}$ with $XY\equiv1\pmod{11}$ (its inverse), and $Y=11\equiv0$ never works. For $X=11\equiv0$ no $Y$ works. So there are $10$ winning outcomes for Joe.

**Answer: $\frac{10}{121}$**

dmm-2011-team-06.title: Follow the first few steps
dmm-2011-team-06.body:
$3^{2011}\to3^{2010}+2$. This is $2$ mod $3$, so next $\lfloor3\log_3(3^{2010}+2)\rfloor$; since $3^{2010}<3^{2010}+2<3^{2010}\cdot(1+10^{-900})$, the logarithm is slightly above $2010$ and $3\log_3(\cdot)$ is slightly above $6030$, giving $6030$.

Then: $6030$ is divisible by $3$: $\frac{6030}3+2=2012$. Next $2012$ is not divisible by $3$, and $3^6=729<2012<3^7=2187$ with $\log_32012\approx6.92$, so $\lfloor3\cdot6.92\rfloor=20$. Then $\lfloor3\log_320\rfloor=\lfloor8.18\rfloor=8$, $\lfloor3\log_38\rfloor=\lfloor5.68\rfloor=5$, $\lfloor3\log_35\rfloor=\lfloor4.39\rfloor=4$, $\lfloor3\log_34\rfloor=\lfloor3.79\rfloor=3$, and finally $3\to\frac33+2=3$.

The sequence is $3^{2011},3^{2010}+2,6030,2012,20,8,5,4,3,3,\dots$, which reaches $3$ after $8$ steps and stays there. After $2011$ steps the number is $3$.

**Answer: 3**

dmm-2011-team-07.title: Solve the self-similar fraction
dmm-2011-team-07.body:
Let $c=4a_n^2-1$ and $x=a_{n+1}$. The fraction repeats itself after the first $-2$, so $x=\dfrac{c}{-2+x}$, i.e. $x^2-2x-c=0$, so $x=1\pm\sqrt{1+c}=1\pm2a_n$. Since $a_{n+1}$ is positive, $a_{n+1}=1+2a_n$.

Then $a_{n+1}+1=2(a_n+1)$ and $a_1+1=2$, so $a_n+1=2^n$ and $a_n=2^n-1$. Hence $a_{2011}=2^{2011}-1$.

**Answer: $2^{2011}-1$**

dmm-2011-team-08.title: Recurrence
dmm-2011-team-08.body:
Let $g(n)$ be the number of good subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Either $n$ is not in the subset ($g(n-1)$ ways) or it is, and then $n-1,n-2$ are not, leaving a good subset of $\{1,\dots,n-3\}$ ($g(n-3)$ ways). So $g(n)=g(n-1)+g(n-3)$ with $g(0)=1,g(1)=2,g(2)=3$.

$g(3)=4,\ g(4)=6,\ g(5)=9,\ g(6)=13,\ g(7)=19,\ g(8)=28,\ g(9)=41,\ g(10)=60,\ g(11)=88,\ g(12)=129,\ g(13)=189.$

**Answer: 189**

dmm-2011-team-08.title: Count by size
dmm-2011-team-08.body:
A good subset with $k$ elements corresponds to choosing $k$ numbers from $13-2(k-1)=15-2k$ (subtract $0,2,4,\dots$ from the sorted elements to make them distinct): $\binom{15-2k}{k}$ ways. Sum over $k=0,\dots,5$:
$$1+13+55+84+35+1=189.$$

**Answer: 189**

dmm-2011-team-09.title: Factor out the gcd
dmm-2011-team-09.body:
Let $g=\gcd(a,b)$ and $a=gx$, $b=gy$ with $\gcd(x,y)=1$. Then $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=gxy$ and the equation becomes $10gxy=g^2(x^2+y^2)$, i.e. $10xy=g(x^2+y^2)$.

Since $\gcd(x,y)=1$, $x^2+y^2$ is coprime to $x$ and to $y$ (a prime dividing $x$ and $x^2+y^2$ would divide $y$), hence coprime to $xy$. So $x^2+y^2\mid10$. With $x\le y$ the only options are $x^2+y^2=2$ ($x=y=1$) and $x^2+y^2=5$ ($x=1,y=2$) and $x^2+y^2=10$ ($x=1,y=3$).

* $(1,1)$: $10=2g$, $g=5$: $(a,b)=(5,5)$.
* $(1,2)$: $20=5g$, $g=4$: $(4,8)$.
* $(1,3)$: $30=10g$, $g=3$: $(3,9)$.

**Answer: $(3,9),(4,8),(5,5)$**

dmm-2011-team-10.title: A recurrence
dmm-2011-team-10.body:
Let $S_m=g(1)+\cdots+g(2^m)$. Among $1,\dots,2^m$ there are $2^{m-1}$ odd numbers, with sum $(2^{m-1})^2=4^{m-1}$, and each odd number is its own largest odd divisor. For an even number $2j$ we have $g(2j)=g(j)$, and $j$ runs over $1,\dots,2^{m-1}$, contributing $S_{m-1}$.

So $S_m=4^{m-1}+S_{m-1}$ with $S_0=g(1)=1$. Therefore
$$S_m=1+(1+4+\cdots+4^{m-1})=1+\frac{4^m-1}{3}=\frac{4^m+2}{3}.$$
For $m=2011$: $\dfrac{4^{2011}+2}{3}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{4^{2011}+2}{3}$**
